note: The right tail of the length distribution (RI-LOR03 §1: p90 ~1,700, max ~4,500). A corpus whose longest book is nine hundred words has the wrong shape whatever its quality, and the shape is what makes a library feel like a library rather than a set of lore entries. `The Commonplace Book of Ivo Sarn` is the `item_ivo_sarns_book` that mainline-act3 names as a `channel: book` source for rev_sarn_flows, and it did not exist. The naturalist survey over-generalises from two observations and names a rival; the romance is set in a province its author has not visited and is beloved.

books.title: Of the Beasts of the Southern Marsh, and Their Dispositions
books.author: Magistra Ivrenne Talloc, of the College at Wayrest, sometime of Gideon
books.unreliability: A first-rate observer and a reckless generaliser. Four of her seven chapters rest on two sightings each, she says so herself in the preface, and the reader forgets by chapter three.
books.text:
PREFACE, WHICH THE READER WILL SKIP AND SHOULD NOT.

I spent four years in this province and I saw a very great deal, and I want to say at the outset, in a place where it cannot be edited out, that four years is nothing. A naturalist in the Gold Coast may see a hundred of a thing in a season. I saw two of several of the animals in this book. Two. Where I have seen two I have said two, in the chapter, and I ask the reader to hold on to it, because I know exactly what happens to a qualification once it is three pages behind you.

CHAPTER THE FIRST. OF THE SLITHERFANG.

The common serpent of the rootlands, and the animal every visitor asks about, chiefly because of the size, which is exaggerated everywhere and does not need to be. The largest I measured was eleven feet and the largest I saw was longer than the boat and I did not measure it.

It is not aggressive and it is not shy; it is indifferent, which frightens people more. It will lie across a path and let a party step over it. It strikes at what moves at the speed of a swimming thing, and a walking man does not move at that speed, and this is the whole of the reason visitors are not bitten more often. A man wading is bitten. A man walking is not. I have watched a poler step over the same animal twice in an afternoon and I have watched the same animal take a swimming rat from four feet without visible preparation.

The venom is not the danger. The danger is the constriction that follows, and the sequence is always the same, and a party that knows the sequence loses nobody.

CHAPTER THE SECOND. OF THE VORIPLASM.

And here I must ask the reader's forbearance, because I saw two.

Both were in the Deep Marshes. Both appeared where deep mud had been disturbed, and both appeared quickly — within the time it takes to walk a hundred paces — and neither pursued us when we left the disturbed ground. On the second occasion my guide, who would not go back into that region for any money afterwards, said only that they come to the digging.

From these two occasions I concluded, and I set it out in the first edition as a settled matter, that the voriplasm is a scavenging form that follows disturbance and that it does not occur outside the Deep Marshes. I have since had letters from three correspondents, one of them uncivil, reporting the animal at Thornmarsh and at the Clay Moor. I do not withdraw the observation. I withdraw the word does not, which was not an observation, it was a flourish, and it was the only interesting thing in the chapter and that is exactly why I wrote it.

What I will still say. It does not eat. I opened both and there was nothing in either that could be called a gut, and no residue of anything, and I have never had an answer to this from anybody. A thing that moves toward disturbance and does not eat is doing something, and I do not know what, and neither does Serjo Fals Rethan, whose remarks on the subject in his second volume are the remarks of a man who has read about an animal.

CHAPTER THE THIRD. OF THE SHELL-BEETLE OF THE THICKET.

Three feet at the shoulder, which is what everyone writes down, and much the more interesting fact is the second one: they do not go into water above the joint of the leg, ever, and there is no water in this province that a thing three feet high cannot cross. They will walk a mile round a puddle. I have followed one doing it.

The local people harvest the shell in the third year and not before, and they know the year by the ridging, and I could not learn to read the ridging in four years of asking. This is not secrecy. Three separate people tried patiently to teach me and all three eventually said the same sentence, which was: you are looking at it.

CHAPTER THE FOURTH. OF THE BIRDS, AND OF WHERE THERE ARE NONE.

The province is loud with birds. There are eleven species I could name in the Blackwood alone before breakfast, and the dawn on the coast road is genuinely difficult to sleep through.

In the Deep Marshes there are none.

Not few. None. I walked four days in that region and did not hear one, and I was listening, because I noticed the absence on the first afternoon and could not stop noticing it. There is no shortage of what a bird eats there. There is no predator I could identify that would account for it. The region is not small and its edges are not sharp; the birds thin over about half a day's walk and then they are simply gone.

I asked everyone I could. A carter at Tenmarch said the water is bad. A rootkeeper said the birds went when the trees stopped talking, which I record as given. A Legion serjeant told me, with complete confidence, that the birds are taken by the voriplasm, which cannot be true, because the voriplasm does not eat.

Three explanations, three people who believed them, and no two of them compatible. I put this down as the single most Argonian fact in my four years, and I mean that as praise: it is a country in which everybody has an answer and none of the answers has ever been checked against another one.

CHAPTER THE FIFTH. OF THE FISH THAT ARE EATEN.

I have given this chapter its own place because it is the only one with any commercial use and because the College will otherwise ask me what I did with the grant. The rice-fish, the black eel, the shore-crab, the fry that are taken in the weirs in the second month. Sizes, seasons, and the four that are poisonous, of which two are eaten anyway after a preparation I describe and would not attempt.

CHAPTER THE SIXTH. OF THE DOMESTIC ANIMALS, OF WHICH THERE ARE NONE WORTH THE NAME.

There is no draught animal in this province. None. Nothing pulls anything. Every load in Black Marsh is carried on a pole, on a barge, or on a back, and the consequence of this runs through everything — there is no wheeled road because there is nothing to pull a wheel, and there is no wheeled road because there is nowhere to put one, and I could not in four years establish which of those came first and I no longer believe the question is well formed.

CHAPTER THE SEVENTH. OF THE HIST, WHICH IS NOT A BEAST AND IS NOT MY SUBJECT.

I shall say one thing and then stop, because the subject has eaten better scholars than me.

A tree does not have a disposition. I have written six chapters on the dispositions of animals, by which I mean the regularities of their behaviour, and a regularity is a thing you can predict from. In four years I could predict the slitherfang, the beetle, the eel and the tick, and I could not predict a Hist once, and I do not mean that its behaviour was complex. I mean that on the eleven occasions I was near one and something happened, the something was different every time, and no two of the eleven have anything in common that I have been able to name.

A naturalist's proper response to that is to say that eleven is not enough observations, and I say it, and I want it in this book that I do not believe it.

books.title: The Lizard-King's Bride: A Romance of the Steaming South
books.author: "A Lady of Quality" (Coriolus Bant, of Bravil)
books.unreliability: Nonsense from the first line to the last, written by a man in Bravil who has never been further south than the Larsius, and it has sold more copies in this province than every other book in it put together.
books.wrong_on_purpose: There are no kings in Black Marsh, no thrones, no marble, no consorts, no court. Argonians in it behave like Colovian courtiers with tails. The province finds it hilarious and buys it anyway.
books.text:
CHAPTER THE FIRST, in which Lady Amaryllis is Taken.

The ship had been three days becalmed upon the wine-dark Topal when the war-canoes came.

Amaryllis Valerian, only daughter of the Count of Chorrol, had never in her nineteen years beheld a Saxhleel, and she beheld eleven of them at once, rising from the water on every side, their scales gleaming emerald and jet in the pitiless southern sun, their spears held with a savage grace that no drilling-master of the Legion could have taught.

She did not scream. Amaryllis Valerian had never screamed in her life, and she did not begin now, and the tallest of them — a warrior of prodigious stature, his crest chased with gold, a scar running from brow to jaw like a river through a marsh — regarded her with something she would afterwards be unable to name.

"This one does not fear," he said, in Tamrielic more perfect than her father's chaplain's.

"This one," said Amaryllis, "is deciding."

CHAPTER THE FOURTH, in which the Palace of Xul-Vaneer is Described.

Of the marble city of Xul-Vaneer, hidden these four thousand years in the green heart of the marsh, it is not possible to write adequately, and the present author will therefore attempt it.

Imagine a Cyrodilic palace of the high Reman style, and then imagine it built of a stone so white that the eye cannot rest upon it at noon, standing upon a hundred terraces above a lake of black water, its every column wound about with flowering vine, its every hall open to the perfumed air. Imagine fountains. Imagine, in each fountain, a fish of gold.

At the summit of the hundred terraces stands the Throne of Roots, and upon the Throne of Roots sits the Lizard-King, and the Lizard-King is Sees-The-Storm-Coming, and Sees-The-Storm-Coming is the warrior of the emerald scales, and Amaryllis Valerian, in a gown of spider-silk that the handmaidens of the palace had wound about her in the manner of the country, ascended those terraces one at a time with her chin up and her heart, if the truth be told, in a state.

CHAPTER THE NINTH, in which there is a Betrothal, and a Storm.

"You have been three months in my house," said the King, "and you have not once asked me for your freedom."

"I have not once been denied it," said Amaryllis. "That is not the same as having it."

The King laughed — a sound like water over stones, the present author has been told — and rose from the Throne of Roots, and the whole of that vast hall was very still.

"My Council would have me marry a daughter of the Nine Tribes," he said. "My Council has never been becalmed on the Topal."

"Your Council," said Amaryllis, "is quite right, and I am going to say so once, and then I am never going to say it again."

Outside, over the black lake, the first of the great rains of the season broke upon the hundred terraces, and every fountain in the city rang.

AFTERWORD BY THE PUBLISHER, added to the eleventh printing.

The present house has received a quantity of correspondence regarding this work, chiefly from the province in which it is set, and the more temperate portion of it may be summarised as follows.

That there is no marble in Black Marsh. That there are no kings in Black Marsh, no thrones, no councils, no crowns, no consorts and no palaces, and that the political arrangements of the interior are such that a correspondent at Helstrom describes the very idea of a Lizard-King as, and we quote him exactly, a question nobody there has ever been bored enough to ask. That there is no city of Xul-Vaneer, and that the name means, in the tongue of the country, something between root-money and paid-for-underneath, which our correspondent describes as the funniest thing he has read in his life.

That Argonians do not have crests. That gowns of spider-silk would, in that climate, and here our correspondent becomes technical.

The present house notes these communications with respect and observes, in mitigation, that the eleventh printing is the eleventh, that the twelfth is at the press, and that of the eleven printings the largest single order in the history of this house — four hundred and sixty copies, paid in advance, on a bond drawn at Gideon — came from a bookseller at Lilmoth who has ordered again twice.

CHAPTER THE FOURTEENTH, in which the Champion of the Nine Tribes Makes his Challenge.

He came up the hundred terraces at dawn, and the whole city came out to watch him come, and he did not hurry.

His name was Breaks-The-Ninth-Rope and he was black where the King was emerald, and he carried no spear, and he had killed, the handmaidens whispered to Amaryllis, eleven men in single combat and never once been marked.

"You have taken a dry woman into the root-house," he said, at the foot of the Throne. "The Nine Tribes did not send me to ask why. The Nine Tribes sent me to end it."

And Amaryllis Valerian, daughter of the Count of Chorrol, who had by now been three seasons in the marble city and had learned a very great deal, stepped down from the King's right hand before the King could rise, and said:

"Then end it with me."

The hall did not laugh. That was the thing she would remember for the rest of her life, when the marble and the fountains and the golden fish had all gone soft in her memory: that a hall of eight hundred warriors of the marsh, who had every reason in the world to laugh, did not.

CHAPTER THE NINETEENTH, and Last, in which there is a Ship.

"Your father's ship stands off the bar," said the King. "It has stood there four days. It will stand there four more and then it will go, and I have given orders that it is not to be troubled either way."

"And if I go down to it?"

"Then you go down to it," said Sees-The-Storm-Coming, "and I do not come to the water to watch, because I am not a man who can be looked at while that is happening."

The rain had begun again over the hundred terraces. It would not stop now until the turn of the year; she knew that, she had learned the seasons of that country as she had learned its speech, badly and completely.

"You have never once," said Amaryllis, "asked me to stay."

"No," said the King.

"Why?"

And the Lizard-King of Xul-Vaneer, master of the Throne of Roots, before whom eight hundred spears went down, looked at the rain on the black lake and said, in a voice she had not heard from him before:

"Because you would."

HERE ENDS THE LIZARD-KING'S BRIDE.

FURTHER TO THE PUBLISHER'S AFTERWORD, appended at the fourteenth printing.

We are able, at last, to print in full the letter of our correspondent the bookseller of Lilmoth, who has now ordered nine hundred and forty copies of this work in six years and who has been asked, repeatedly and by several parties, to explain himself.

"You keep writing to ask whether we know it is nonsense. Sirs. We know.

"There is no marble. There are no kings. There is no city and the name of your city is a joke that has been going round three settlements for four years and is not getting old. Your author has put crests on us. Your author thinks we have a Council.

"I sell it because there is a girl in it who is taken to a place she does not understand and who does not scream and does not thank anybody and does not go home, and because there is not one other book in the whole of your Empire's printing in which one of us is looked at for four hundred pages by somebody who is trying to work out what we are, rather than what we are for.

"Send the twelfth. Send four hundred. And tell your author that a poler at Gideon has read chapter nine aloud on a barge to eleven people who could not read it themselves, twice, and that the second time was because they asked."

books.title: The Commonplace Book of Sexton Ivo Sarn
books.author: Ivo Sarn, sexton of the Drowned Court, and nobody was meant to read this
books.unreliability: A private working book. It is not written to be understood, it is written to be sufficient for the one person who already knows what it is about, and it assumes an enormous amount that it never says.
books.text:
A working book. Sums at the back. Do not lend.

— Third salt pan. Ring is dead on a line running about NNE, four hundred paces followed, did not follow further, boots.

— Six throats found. Numbered them in the order I found them and I now regret that, because it is not the order they run in.

— Draw at the Ladder, turn of the tide: 4. Draw at Soulrest same hour: 4. Draw at Hollow-Reeds same hour: 4. Three wells thirty miles apart giving the same figure to the notch on the same day is not three wells. It is one thing with three taps on it.

— Repeated the above on four separate days. Same. Once got 4 / 4 / 3 and the 3 was Hollow-Reeds and it had rained.

— Which is the point. It rained upstream of Hollow-Reeds and Hollow-Reeds went DOWN. If the wells were drinking rain the rain would put them up.

— So they are not drinking what falls on them. They are drinking what gets past something.

— Went out to the second throat with a line and a float. Bore narrows at about eleven feet to something worked. Cannot see it. Float will not pass. Poked at it with a pole for an hour like an idiot.

— Note for whoever finds this: the throats are NOT the intakes. The throats are the vents. The intakes are lower and I have never seen one and I am reasoning about them from the vents, and if I am wrong about this then everything after here is wrong too.

— Sums, first attempt. If the return at a well is what the machine lets past, and the machine's allowance is fixed, then the return per death falls when the deaths rise and holds when they hold. Test: the fever year. Deaths up by a third. Return per death down by about a third. It fits.

— It fits too well and I do not trust it. Checked against the salt year. Deaths up by more than a third and the return per death down by only a fifth. Does not fit.

— Unless the allowance is not fixed. Unless the allowance drifts.

— Second attempt at the sums, allowing the allowance to drift. Then the whole four hundred years comes out as one curve with a shoulder in it at about the thirty-ninth year, and the shoulder is where the drift starts, and everything before the shoulder is flat.

— Hosk-Vei has the same shoulder from the Tally and he got there by adding and I got there by measuring three wells with a float, and neither of us has told the other. He would say I have fitted a curve to a story. He would be right to say it.

— The thing I cannot get round and have written out four times to see if it looks better: if the allowance is drifting DOWN, then something below the allowance is taking MORE. Not the cutting. The cutting is above. This is below.

— And if it is below then closing a throat does not stop it. Closing a throat stops what comes UP. It does nothing at all to what goes DOWN, and the wells are the up.

— Which means the thing everyone will want to do — go down there and shut it — makes the wells worse before it makes them anything, and I would like somebody cleverer than me to tell me I am wrong about that.

— Went to Rell. Did not tell her about the float. Asked her a general question about the Court's position and got a general answer. She knows something. Everybody in that counting house knows something and none of them knows the same thing and none of them will say what it is, and I am beginning to think that is not a conspiracy, I think it is eleven people each assuming they are the one who is behind.

— Sixth throat. Different. Worked stone at the throat is cut, not cast — chisel work, and recent chisel work, within a generation. Somebody has been down there and made it narrower.

— Somebody has been maintaining it.

— I have not written that anywhere else and I am not going to say it to anyone until I have been back and looked again, because if I am right about the chisel work then the whole thing is not a ruin, and if it is not a ruin then there is a difference between a machine that is failing and a machine that is being adjusted, and I do not want to be the man who says that out loud in Soulrest and turns out to have seen a scratch.

— Going back on the ninth. Taking the long line and the good lamp. Told Doun where I am going, which is the first sensible thing in this book.

— Back at the sixth. It is chisel work. Not a scratch. Eleven inches of dressed narrowing set into a cast bore, laid in courses like a mason would lay them, and dry-jointed, and the joints are tight enough that I could not get the edge of a knife in.

— Nobody in this province lays dry joint. Nobody has for four hundred years. The Court's own stair is mortared.

— So either it is as old as the rest of it and I am wrong about the tooling, or somebody who knows how to lay dry joint has been down a vent inside a generation with a chisel and a lamp and a reason.

— I want to be careful here because I can feel myself enjoying this.

— Argument against me: a cut face weathers slowly in a dry bore. A face cut four hundred years ago in still air eleven feet down could look like this. Fair. I cannot date stone by looking at it and neither can anyone else who has told me they can.

— Argument for me: the narrowing at the sixth is different from the narrowing at the second and the fourth. Different bore, different depth of set, different hand. If they were all built together they would all be the same. Somebody has been fitting them one at a time over a long period, which is not building, it is tuning.

— And if a thing is being tuned then it is being tuned TO something, and the thing everybody assumes is a ruin is a thing with a setting on it.

— The other reading, which I am writing down so that I have written it down: they are all original, all different because eleven crews built them over eleven seasons the way any large works gets built, and I have made a story out of a mason's tolerance.

— Sums, third attempt, taking the six vents as six settings and letting each one carry a share. Comes out. Comes out better than the second attempt. I do not know whether that means anything or whether I have just given myself another parameter to bend.

— Doun asked me at the yard what I am doing down there and I told him the truth, which is that I am measuring how much water comes up six holes, and he said that sounds like a job for somebody with a rope and I said yes it does.

(Here the entries stop. Four leaves at the back carry sums in Sarn's hand, worked twice, in ink and again in pencil, and the pencil figures are not the same as the ink ones and are not crossed out.)

books.title: A Chronicle of the Duskfall, Assembled from the Sayings of Eleven Keepers
books.author: Teeus-Ahai, of Helstrom, who did the assembling and is not sorry
books.unreliability: Eleven oral accounts, each internally consistent and mutually incompatible, set down side by side by a compiler who refuses to reconcile them and says why. He is also quietly wrong about one thing: he thinks the disagreement is a problem with the sources.

contradicts.on: who built the xanmeers and why the building stopped

books.text:
I was told by the keepers at Helstrom that this should not be written down and I have written it down, and I want to put their reason first so that nobody thinks I did not hear it.

Their reason is that a saying is repaired every time it is said. A keeper who says a thing wrongly is corrected by the one beside her, and the next time she says it right, and this has been going on for as long as there have been two keepers. Writing stops the repairing. What I set down here is eleven accounts as they stood on the day I heard them, and from today they will not improve, and there will be people in a hundred years who prefer this book to a living keeper, and that will be my doing.

I have done it anyway, because there are four keepers left at Helstrom who know the whole of it and when I began there were seven.

WHAT ALL ELEVEN AGREE ON.

That there was a before. That in the before, our people built the stone nests, and built them everywhere, and joined them, and that the joining is the part they are proud of and not the building.

That it ended. Not slowly.

That afterwards nobody knew how to do it, and that this was not a matter of the knowing being lost from books, because there were no books; it was lost from hands.

That the trees were there before, during and after, and that the trees have never said one word about any of it to anybody, and that four of my eleven brought this up unprompted and one of them was angry about it.

WHERE THEY DIVIDE, AND I HAVE PUT THEM IN THE ORDER I HEARD THEM AND NOT IN AN ORDER THAT MAKES A CASE.

The first keeper said the sky went out. She meant it plainly; she said the light failed and did not come back for a length of time she gave as a hatching, which is not a unit anybody else uses, and she would not convert it.

The second keeper said nothing went out and that the first keeper's account is a children's version of the third keeper's.

The third keeper said the water came up. Not a flood — a change of level, everywhere, permanent, and that the lower nests are under it now and that is why the causeways go into the marsh from nothing.

The fourth keeper said the water went down, and that the marsh we live in is what was left when it went, and that the nests are on the high ground because the high ground is where the shore was.

The fifth keeper said it was a sickness, and when I asked whether she meant the Knahaten she was insulted, and said that the Knahaten is a thing that happened to our neighbours in her grandmother's grandmother's time and that I was doing the thing the Imperials do, which is to take the biggest thing we can remember and put it in front of the things we cannot.

The sixth keeper said we stopped because we finished.

I asked her four times, in four ways, over two days. She would not put anything else on it. She said: it was finished, and after a thing is finished you do not go on doing it, and she seemed to find the question stupid, and I have not been able to decide in six years whether that was an evasion or the only answer in this book that nobody has decorated.

The seventh keeper said there was a war and would not say with whom.

The eighth keeper said there was a war and said it was with ourselves, and that the nests are on opposite sides of the water from each other for a reason, and that if I went and looked at which faces which I would see it. I have gone and looked. Two of them do face each other. Nine of them do not face anything.

The ninth keeper is the only one who spoke about the wells. She said the wells came after, that before Duskfall no root was cut, and that the first cutting and the ending are the same event told from two ends. She would not say which end. She is dead now and I did not ask her again and that is the largest single failure of my life.

The tenth keeper said all of the above have happened, and that a people can have more than one ending, and that we are asking which of eleven accounts is true in the manner of somebody who has only ever ended once.

The eleventh keeper — and he was the oldest, and he was not from Helstrom, and he was brought to me by the fourth keeper specifically so that he could say this — said that the question is wrong because it assumes we stopped. He said: look at what we do now. He said we still stack. He said a stilt village is a nest and a barge road is a causeway and a weir is a wall that tells water where to stop, and that we do all of it in reed and mud because reed and mud is what we have, and that a people who lost how to build would not still be building the same shapes out of worse material.

He said: we did not forget how. We forgot what it was for, and you cannot tell the difference from outside, and neither can we.

MY OWN NOTE, WHICH IS SHORT.

A reader will want me to say which of the eleven is right and I am not going to, and I want to be honest about why, which is not humility. It is that I have listened to all eleven and I cannot find the seam. Each of them is complete. Each of them accounts for the nests, the causeways, the marsh and the silence of the trees. If one of them were confused I could pull it. None of them is confused.

What I think — and this is mine and no keeper said it — is that eleven accounts that are each complete and cannot be joined is not eleven damaged copies of one story. It is what a thing looks like when it was too large to be seen from one place, and every one of these accounts is somebody's grandmother telling the truth about her own end of it.

An Imperial would call that a failure of sources. I have met the Imperial who would call it that. He measured eleven buildings with a rod and never once asked what they were standing on.

ADDED SIX YEARS LATER.

There was a twelfth and I did not get it.

The fourth keeper sent for me in the wet of the year I was at Stormhold and I did not go, because I was at Stormhold, and because I had eleven and I thought eleven was a book.

She died in that season. The keepers at Helstrom will not tell me what she wanted to say and I do not think they are being cruel; I think they do not know, and I think that a keeper who sends for a man to say a thing has usually decided that it is not a thing to leave with the person standing next to her.

I am putting this at the back of the book rather than the front because I do not want it read as humility. It is not humility. It is the specific, dateable, avoidable loss of one of twelve accounts of the end of our world, and the reason for it was that I had a fair copy to finish.

books.title: The Poler's Book: the Roads That Are Water
books.author: Eeja-Sul of the Gideon quay, and eleven polers who argued about it
books.unreliability: Reliable, practical, and it contains one route that has not been passable for nine years, which the compiler knows about and has left in because two of the eleven insist it still is.
books.text:
A road in this country is a thing you can be on. That is the whole definition and it is why an Imperial map of Black Marsh is a picture of eight harbours and a lot of blank paper: they draw what is dry, and what is dry here is about a fortieth of what is passable.

This book is the water roads out of Gideon, as eleven of us pole them. Where we disagreed I have put both, with who says which, and the reader may take whichever of us they trust.

HOW YOU ASK.

Every morning you ask. Not the water — the tree, at whichever well you slept nearest, and if you slept nowhere near a well you should not be moving that day and I do not care how far behind you are.

You ask by putting a hand in the water at the well and waiting long enough to be embarrassed. What you get is not words and it is not a picture. It is a direction that you find you have already decided on, and outlanders never believe this and every poler alive has had the day where they went the way they did not fancy and found out at noon why.

A crew that does not ask arrives about as often as a crew that does. The difference is in the years, not the days.

THE GIDEON TO HOLLOW-REEDS ROAD, INLAND WATER.

Out of the market cross by the toll gate cut, which is the only way a loaded barge leaves Gideon, and you will wait, and everybody waits, and the waiting is where you find out what has moved this season.

Out of the cut you are in slow water for the first two hours with willows both sides. Keep the willows on your left. There is a second channel to the right that looks better, is better, and rejoins six miles down at a bar that takes a foot off your draught, and if you are loaded you will sit on it until the wet.

At the willows' end the water opens and you lose your bank. Hold what you had. Count a slow six hundred. You will pick up the withy posts on the left, and the posts run the whole way to the landing at Hollow-Reeds, and they are maintained by the people there and they are the only maintained thing on this road.

Half a day. A day loaded. Nobody has ever been lost on it and it is the road we send the new ones on.

THE COAST TRACK, SOULREST TO GIDEON, WHICH IS NOT A WATER ROAD AND IS IN THIS BOOK BECAUSE PEOPLE ASK.

Walk it. Do not try to pole the shore; the shore is a shore.

North out of Soulrest with the Stone Wastes on your right the whole way. You will know the Wastes when the ground starts sounding wrong under you. Where the coast track meets the Wastes there is a rib of pale stone standing out of the mud that the carters count their days by, and that is the Bone Ladder, and there is a sapwell off the track on the landward side under the rib, and a keeper who will let you sit.

From the Ladder keep the water on your left as far as Hollow-Reeds. Then inland at the willows and you are on the road above.

Four days walking. More if you stop, and you will stop at the Ladder, and everyone on that road can tell you where the Ladder is.

THE UPPER REACH, TOWARD THE FALLS.

This is the one to be careful about and it is the one this book argues about.

You hear the Border Falls a very long time before you see them, and the hearing is the navigation: as long as they are ahead and to your right, you are in the channel. When they come round to your right ear entirely, you have gone into the loop and you must come back out of the loop, and the loop looks exactly like the channel and is four hours long.

Above the loop there was a passage through to the eastern water. Sesh-Weth and Ojal say it is still there and that they took a light barge through it two seasons ago. Nine of us say it closed nine years ago when the bank came down in the wet and that what those two went through was the loop, at high water, in the dark, and got lucky and have been telling everyone ever since.

I have put it in because they insisted and because I said I would put in what people said. I have not been through it. I will not be going.

TIDE-POLES.

On any tideway there are poles with the waterline painted. The paint is the passable line and not the high line — that is the mistake — and a tideway with the water above the paint is not slow, it is shut, and a poler who goes on because it is only a hand above the paint is the reason we paint them.

The poles are maintained by whoever lives nearest and are therefore honest at Stilt-Row, optimistic at Mudwater Landing, and a work of fiction at the kiln camp, where they have been painting the same pole for eleven years without looking at it.

WHAT TO DO IF YOU ARE LOST.

Stop. Tie up. This is the whole of the advice and it is the advice every drowned poler ignored.

Water in this country does not go anywhere useful just because it is going. A channel that is moving is not a channel that is going to the sea; half the water in the rootlands is going round in a circle two days wide. If you do not know where you are, you will not learn it by moving, and you will use up the light, and the light is the only thing you actually have.

Tie up. Sleep. Ask in the morning.

THE THORN ROAD, WHICH IS NOT ONE ROAD.

Everybody says the Thorn road as though there were a Thorn road. There are three and which one exists depends on the season, and a poler who has done it in the wet and thinks he has done it has done a different journey to the one he will do in the dry.

In the wet, you go over the thicket flats, which are under two feet of water and are the easiest poling in the province, and you go in a straight line, and you arrive in a day and a half and wonder what everyone complains about.

In the dry, the flats are mud and the mud will not take a pole and will not take a foot either. Then it is the stem channels, which is a full three days of turning, and the knife-marks cut into the stems are the only navigation there is and they are cut for people who already know the road. Two marks together is a turning. One mark is keep on. A mark with a cut across it is do not, and the reason for the do-not has usually gone away by the time you get there and occasionally has not.

Between the two, in the fortnight when the flats are neither, nobody goes, and Thorn is on its own for that fortnight every year and has been as long as there has been a Thorn.

HAZARDS, IN THE ORDER THEY ACTUALLY KILL PEOPLE.

First, the sun. More polers have been finished by three days in the open on a slow reach than by everything else in this list put together. Rig the mat. Rig it even when you are only going as far as the bar.

Second, the load. A barge that is loaded high is not slower, it is differently balanced, and it turns over at the moment you push against it hardest, which is the moment you have decided to correct something.

Third, salt water in the tideways at the turn. Not for you — for the drinking barrel, which will be brackish and which you will not notice until the second day, and which will put a crew on their backs a long way from anywhere.

Fourth, the animals, and they are fourth, and every outlander puts them first. In eleven of us there is one bite between us in a hundred and forty years of poling, and it happened in the water and not on the barge, and the man is alive.

Fifth, other people. This is fifth on the water roads and it is first on the coast track and that is the whole difference between the two and is why we pole.
